etymology: From Old English weorold, a compound of wer (man) and eld (age) — literally the age of man, the span of human generations. The English word therefore began as a word about time and only afterward became a word about place, and Scripture uses it in both senses at once. Greek kosmos means an ordered arrangement, an adornment (whence cosmetic); Greek aiōn means an age or era. The King James Version renders both by world, which is why the same English word can mean the creation God made and loves, and the present evil order the believer is forbidden to love.
biblical_def: World in Scripture carries three distinct senses which must never be collapsed into one another. First, it is the created order as God made it and still owns it: “The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein” (Psa 24:1). There is no square inch of it that is not His, and no part of it evil in itself. Second, it is the mass of humanity, the race of men considered as the object of God's saving purpose: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son” (Joh 3:16). Third — and this is the sense the believer must learn to hear — it is the present order of things organised in rebellion against God, the age with its own wisdom, its own honours, and its own prince. Of this world Christ said of His own, “They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world” (Joh 17:16). The three senses stand together without contradiction: God made the world, God loves the world of men, and God's people are strangers to the world as a system. The peril of the Christian life is that the third sense is invisible to those inside it. A man does not feel worldly; he feels normal. Hence the searching question, “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mat 16:26) — the whole world being, on the accounting of eternity, a losing trade.
webster_summary: The created universe and the earth; the inhabitants of the earth, mankind; and in the Scripture sense, the present course and system of human affairs as it stands opposed to God, together with its cares, honours, and pleasures.
webster_full: WORLD, n. 1. The universe; the whole system of created things; the whole creation of God, visible and invisible.
2. The earth; the terraqueous globe, with all it contains; sometimes limited to one of its great divisions, as the old world and the new.
3. The inhabitants of the earth; the whole human race. God so loved the world. John 3.
4. Present state of existence; the course of secular affairs, as distinguished from the life to come. The cares of this world choke the word. Matt. 13.

5. The customs, maxims and manners of men, considered as opposed to the spirit and law of the gospel; that system of things by which men live without God. Love not the world. 1 John 2. Be not conformed to this world. Rom. 12.
corruption_summary: Worldliness is redefined as cultural engagement, so that conformity to the age is rebranded a missionary virtue; and at the other extreme, the goodness of the created world is denied outright, as though matter itself were the enemy.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest modern corruption is to make the third sense of world disappear. Because Joh 3:16 says God loved the world, it is argued that the believer's posture toward the world must be simple affirmation, and every call to separation is treated as fear, tribalism, or a failure of love. The argument works only by equivocation: the world God loved is the world of men, and He loved it by sending His Son to die for sinners in it — not by approving the system that crucified Him. Scripture holds both without embarrassment: friendship with the world is enmity with God, and yet the Son came to save the world. What the equivocation produces in practice is a church indistinguishable from the age it was sent to convert, which has never yet converted anybody. Be not conformed to this world is a command, and it presupposes that conformity is the default and the current runs one way.

The opposite error is older and equally serious: the Gnostic and ascetic instinct that treats the material creation itself as the corruption, so that holiness means withdrawal from matter, marriage, food, property, and the ordinary callings. Scripture forbids this in the strongest terms — every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. The world as creation is the LORD's and is declared very good; the world as system is passing away. The Christian is therefore neither a conformist nor a hermit but a stranger and a pilgrim who uses this world without abusing it, holding it loosely because its fashion passeth away, and holding it gratefully because its Maker made it.
roots_summary: Hebrew tēbēl is the habitable, fruitful earth; cheled is the world as a fleeting duration. Greek kosmos is the ordered creation and, by extension, the ordered human system in rebellion; aiōn is the present age as against the age to come.
roots_lines: Hebrew tēbēl (H8398) — the habitable and productive earth, the world as fruitful ground; used in Psa 24:1 and Psa 90:2.
Hebrew cheled (H2465) — the world regarded as a lifetime or fleeting duration; mine age is as nothing before thee (Psa 39:5).
Greek kosmos (G2889) — order, adornment, the ordered universe; then the inhabitants of it; then the organised system opposed to God (Joh 17:16).
Greek aiōn (G165) — an age, era, or course of time; rendered world in the end of the world and the cares of this world.
Greek oikoumenē (G3625) — the inhabited earth, the settled and civilised world; whence the taxing of all the world in Luk 2:1.
usage: Of the creation God owns: the earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein (Psa 24:1).
Of the race God loved and redeemed: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son (Joh 3:16).
Of the system the believer is not of: they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world (Joh 17:16).
scriptures: Psalm 24:1
A Psalm of David. The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.
John 3:16
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
John 17:16
They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
Matthew 16:26
For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?

etymology: From Old French contree, from Latin contrata, that which lies over against the beholder — the land spread out before one's eyes. The idea in the root is the land as seen from where a man stands, and so the word carries naturally both the land a man belongs to and the land he is looking toward. Scripture uses it in both directions at once: the country a man is called to leave, and the better country he is travelling to.
biblical_def: Country in Scripture is rarely a merely geographical word; it is a word about belonging, and therefore about faith. The life of faith begins with a command to leave one: “Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee” (Gen 12:1). Everything a man's identity rests on — his nation, his clan, his household — is named and surrendered before the promise is even described. The whole of Hebrews 11 then reads that departure as the pattern of all believing: “For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country” (Heb 11:14). The patriarchs died in faith without receiving the promises, and the writer will not let us think they were merely homesick for Mesopotamia — had they been, they had opportunity to return. What they sought was elsewhere: “But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city” (Heb 11:16). Against that stands the far country of the prodigal, the country a man goes to in order to be away from his father: “took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luk 15:13). Two journeys, then, run through Scripture — out of a country toward God, and into a far country away from Him — and every man is on one of them.
webster_summary: A tract of land, region, or district; the territory of a nation; the rural parts as distinguished from the town; and the land of one's birth or citizenship, whence the Scripture's better country, which is heavenly.
webster_full: COUNTRY, n. 1. Properly, the land lying about or near a city; the parts of a region at a distance from a town.
2. A tract of land, or region of indefinite extent; as the hill country, the country of Moab.
3. The kingdom, state or territory in which one is born, or of which one is a citizen; native land.
4. The inhabitants of a region or state taken collectively; as, the whole country rose against him.
5. In Scripture, a better country, that is, an heavenly; the region of the blessed, sought by faith. Heb. 11.
corruption_summary: The heavenly country is emptied of its content and reduced to a metaphor for social improvement here, so that the pilgrim character of the Christian life is lost; or, at the opposite extreme, earthly country is absolutised until patriotism becomes a rival religion.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the quiet deletion of the better country. Where the hope of an actual prepared city is treated as pre-modern imagery for a renewed society in this age, the whole logic of Hebrews 11 collapses: the patriarchs become men who wanted a better Canaan rather than men who confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. Scripture will not permit the reduction. God has prepared for them a city — a real one, prepared by a real act, for real persons who died without seeing it. Strip that out and Christian endurance loses its object, and suffering loses its proportion; for it is precisely the weight of the country to come that makes the afflictions of the present time light. A gospel that promises only a better version of here has nothing to say at a graveside.

The opposite corruption absolutises the earthly country. A man's nation is a real gift and a real obligation — Scripture honours the love of one's people, and Paul could wish himself accursed for his kinsmen according to the flesh — but the moment the nation becomes the highest loyalty it becomes an idol, and an idol that has repeatedly demanded blood. The believer holds his citizenship here genuinely and holds it second. Our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour. That ordering does not weaken a man's service to his country; it is the only thing that keeps such service from becoming worship, and the only thing that gives him a standard by which to call his own nation to repentance when it needs it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'erets is land, earth, or country, the commonest word for territory; sādeh is open field or countryside as against the walled town. Greek chōra is a region or district, and patris is the fatherland or native place.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'erets (H776) — earth, land, country; the ordinary word for a territory, as get thee out of thy country (Gen 12:1).
Hebrew sādeh (H7704) — field, open country, the land outside the city wall; rendered country in the men of the country.
Greek chōra (G5561) — region, district, the country as against the city; a far country in Luk 15:13.
Greek patris (G3968) — fatherland, native place; a prophet is not without honour, save in his own country (Mat 13:57).
Greek kreittōn patris epouranios — the better country, that is, an heavenly, of Heb 11:16; the object of patriarchal faith.
usage: Of the country to be left at God's call: get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred (Gen 12:1).
Of the country sought by faith: they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly (Heb 11:16).
Of the far country of the prodigal: took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance (Luk 15:13).
scriptures: Genesis 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
Hebrews 11:14
For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country.
Hebrews 11:16
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
Luke 15:13
And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.

etymology: From Old French bordure, an edge or brim, from a Frankish root meaning board or side. The Hebrew g'būl is stronger than the English suggests: it means not merely an edge but a bound set, a limit fixed by authority, and the same word does duty for the boundary of a field, the frontier of a nation, and the shore that bounds the sea. Behind every biblical border stands the One who set it.
biblical_def: A border in Scripture is a divine appointment before it is a human survey. The inheritance of each tribe was allotted by lot before the LORD, and its borders were therefore not negotiable lines but sacred trusts, which is why removing one was a covenant crime and not merely a property dispute: “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance” (Deu 19:14). Proverbs repeats it as a maxim of the wise: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). The stone in the ground stood for something no man had the right to move, and a nation that begins moving its stones has begun dissolving. Because the borders are God's, He is free to enlarge them, and He promises to do so precisely when His people are most exposed by obedience: “For I will cast out the nations before thee, and enlarge thy borders: neither shall any man desire thy land, when thou shalt go up to appear before the LORD thy God thrice in the year” (Exo 34:24) — the men leave the frontier undefended three times a year to worship, and God undertakes the defence Himself. And peace within the borders is His gift, not the achievement of statecraft: “He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the finest of the wheat” (Psa 147:14). God fixes bounds, God enlarges them, God keeps them.
webster_summary: The outer edge or extremity of anything; the boundary or frontier of a territory; the ancient landmark set by the fathers, which Scripture forbids to remove; and the ornamental hem or fringe of a garment.
webster_full: BORDER, n. 1. The outer edge of any thing; the brim, margin, or extremity.
2. The exterior limit of a country, province, or estate; the confine or frontier; as, the borders of a kingdom.
3. A boundary mark; the landmark set of old time in an inheritance. Deut. 19.
4. The hem, fringe, or ornamental edge of a garment; as the border of his garment, which the woman touched. Matt. 9.
5. In Scripture, the bounds of a people's habitation, appointed by God. He hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation. Acts 17.
corruption_summary: Every boundary is treated as an arbitrary construction of power to be dissolved, so that limits of nation, property, office, and sex are all read as oppression rather than as the fixed appointments of a wise Creator.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is that a border is a wound. Because some borders have been drawn unjustly — and some certainly have — it is inferred that boundedness itself is the injustice, and the moral energy of an age goes into erasure. Scripture's testimony runs the other way: God determined the times before appointed and the bounds of men's habitation, and He did it so that they should seek the Lord. The limit is an instrument of mercy. The same God who set the shore against the sea — hitherto shalt thou come, but no further — sets bounds to nations, to households, to offices, and to the creational distinction of male and female, and in every case the bound is what makes the thing inside it able to flourish. A field without edges is not a larger field; it is not a field at all.

The corruption has a second and quieter form: not the dissolving of borders by ideology but the moving of them by greed. Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark is aimed at the strong man who shifts a stone by a foot each year, and the prophets name it among the sins that bring judgment — the princes of Judah were like them that remove the bound. It is the sin of encroachment, and it is respectable because it is gradual. It applies wherever appointed limits are quietly annexed: a magistrate absorbing the authority of the family, a church annexing the conscience Scripture leaves free, an employer taking the day God reserved. Recovering the border means recovering the fear of God in small increments, since it is by small increments that landmarks move.
roots_summary: Hebrew g'būl is a bound, boundary, or territory, and by metonymy the land enclosed; qātseh is an extremity or end. Greek horion is a boundary or coast, and gives the verb horizō, to mark off or determine.
roots_lines: Hebrew g'būl (H1366) — boundary, border, territory; the fixed limit of an inheritance, and by extension the inheritance itself.
Hebrew g'būlāh (H1367) — a bound or landmark, the feminine form used of the borders of the tribes in Joshua.
Hebrew qātseh (H7097) — end, extremity, uttermost part; from the uttermost part of heaven unto the other.
Greek horion (G3725) — a boundary, and in the plural the coasts or borders of a region; the coasts of Tyre and Sidon (Mat 15:21).
Greek horizō (G3724) — to mark out by bounds, to determine or appoint; used of God determining the bounds of men's habitation (Act 17:26).
usage: Of the landmark that may not be moved: thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark (Deu 19:14; Pro 22:28).
Of borders enlarged by God: I will cast out the nations before thee, and enlarge thy borders (Exo 34:24).
Of peace within the borders as God's gift: he maketh peace in thy borders (Psa 147:14).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 19:14
Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance, which thou shalt inherit in the land that the LORD thy God giveth thee to possess it.
Proverbs 22:28
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Exodus 34:24
For I will cast out the nations before thee, and enlarge thy borders: neither shall any man desire thy land, when thou shalt go up to appear before the LORD thy God thrice in the year.
Psalm 147:14
He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the finest of the wheat.

pos: n. and adj. (rendering Hebrew qedem and mizrāch, Greek anatolē)
etymology: From Old English east, of the same root as Latin aurora and Greek ēōs, the dawn — the east being simply where the light comes from. Hebrew has two words and they divide the sense exactly: mizrāch is the place of the rising of the sun, and qedem is what lies in front, since a Hebrew orients himself facing the sunrise, so that east is before, west behind, south on the right hand, north on the left. The same word qedem therefore means ancient and aforetime: in Hebrew, what is ahead of you spatially is what is behind you temporally.
biblical_def: East is the direction of beginnings and of exile, and Scripture uses it with great deliberateness. The garden was planted there: “And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed” (Gen 2:8). When man fell he was driven out, and the guard was set on that side: “he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life” (Gen 3:24). Thereafter movement eastward in Genesis is consistently movement away — Cain dwells east of Eden, the builders of Babel journey from the east, Lot chooses the eastward plain. The tabernacle and temple were entered from the east, so that a worshipper coming in walked westward, back toward the presence he had been driven from; and Ezekiel sees the glory return by the east gate. The gospel keeps the pattern: “there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem” (Mat 2:1), the far nations arriving at the light. And the direction becomes the measure of forgiveness itself, chosen because it is the one axis with no meeting point — north and south terminate at the poles, but east and west never meet: “As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us” (Psa 103:12).
webster_summary: The point of the compass where the sun rises; the quarter of the heavens toward the dawn; and in Scripture the direction of Eden and its guarded gate, of exile, of the coming of the wise men, and of the immeasurable distance to which sin is removed.
webster_full: EAST, n. 1. The point in the heavens where the sun is seen to rise at the equinox, or that point of the horizon lying directly opposite to the west.
2. The regions or countries lying east of any place; the Orient.
3. adj. Toward the rising sun; as the east gate, the east border, the east wind.
4. In Hebrew usage, that which is before or in front, the observer being conceived as facing the sunrise; whence the same word signifies ancient time, or aforetime.
5. In Scripture, a garden eastward in Eden. Gen. 2. Wise men from the east. Matt. 2. As far as the east is from the west. Psalm 103.
corruption_summary: The compass directions are read as borrowed pagan cosmology rather than as the ordinary orientation of a real people in a real land, and the plain historicity of Eden and its guarded gate is dissolved into myth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure on east comes from a different quarter: the habit of treating every orientational detail in Genesis as a literary borrowing from surrounding creation myths, so that the garden eastward, the cherubim at the east, and the eastward drift of Cain and Babel become mythological furniture rather than record. The dictionary takes the narrative as history. Eden was a real place with a real gate, guarded by real cherubim, and the direction is recorded because it happened that way. Where the surrounding nations preserved distorted memories of a lost paradise, that is corroboration of a true event, not the source of a borrowed tale.

The principle to recover is that God orders space as He orders time, and that the ordering preaches. It is not accidental that the way back into the garden was barred on the east and that the way into the tabernacle was opened on the east; the worshipper walking in was walking back along the road man had been driven down, toward a presence now approachable by blood. Nor is Psa 103:12 a piece of poetic vagueness — the psalmist chose the one axis of the compass that has no terminus, and said the distance our transgressions are removed is that one. To read such details as decoration is to miss that Scripture teaches doctrine through the shape of the world, and to lose the comfort the detail was given to carry.
roots_summary: Hebrew mizrāch is the place of the sun's rising; qedem is front, before, and hence both east and ancient time. Greek anatolē is a rising, used of the star in the east and as a title of Christ, the Dayspring from on high.
roots_lines: Hebrew qedem (H6924) — front, that which is before; hence east, and hence also aforetime, of old, everlasting; the God of old is the God of qedem.
Hebrew mizrāch (H4217) — the place of sunrise, the east quarter; from zārach, to rise or shine forth.
Hebrew qādīm (H6921) — the east wind, the scorching sirocco of judgment that blasted Pharaoh's ears of corn (Gen 41:6).
Greek anatolē (G395) — a rising, of the sun or a star; the wise men saw his star in the east, and Zacharias names Christ the Dayspring (Luk 1:78).
Hebrew orientation — facing the sunrise, so that before is east, behind west, the right hand south, and the left hand north (compare Job 23:9).
usage: Of Eden and its guarded gate: a garden eastward in Eden (Gen 2:8); cherubims at the east of the garden (Gen 3:24).
Of the nations coming to the light: there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem (Mat 2:1).
Of the measure of pardon: as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions (Psa 103:12).
scriptures: Genesis 2:8
And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.
Genesis 3:24
So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.
Matthew 2:1
Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem,
Psalm 103:12
As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.

pos: n. and adj. (rendering Hebrew yām and ma'arāb, Greek dusmē)
etymology: From Old English west, cognate with Latin vesper, evening — the west being the quarter of the day's decline. The Hebrew is startlingly concrete: the ordinary word for west is yām, the sea, because for a man standing in Canaan the west simply is the Mediterranean. To say westward in Hebrew is to say seaward. The alternative ma'arāb means the place of the sun's going in, its setting.
biblical_def: West in Scripture is the seaward side, the quarter of the sun's setting, and above all the far end of the axis on which God measures both His mercy and the reach of His gathering. Because Israel's west was the open sea, the word carried the sense of the boundary beyond which the land gave out — the uttermost sea marked the western limit of the promise. The compass is used most memorably as a pair: “As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us” (Psa 103:12), where the two ends of an infinite line stand for a separation between the believer and his sin which no measurement can close. The same pairing then becomes the shape of the gathering of the elect from among the nations. To Israel God promises, “Fear not: for I am with thee: I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west” (Isa 43:5); and Jacob is told his descendants shall “spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south: and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed” (Gen 28:14). The Lord Jesus takes up the same figure and turns it against presumption: “many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 8:11) — strangers from the far quarters seated at the patriarchs' table while the children of the kingdom are cast out.
webster_summary: The point of the compass where the sun sets; in Hebrew idiom the seaward quarter, the Mediterranean lying west of Canaan; and in Scripture one end of the measure of pardon and one quarter from which the redeemed are gathered.
webster_full: WEST, n. 1. That point of the horizon where the sun sets at the equinox; the point opposite to the east.
2. The region of the heavens or of the earth lying toward the setting sun; the occident.
3. adj. Being in a line toward the setting sun; as the west border, the west side.
4. In Hebrew usage, the sea; the Mediterranean lying westward of Canaan, whence seaward and westward are one word.
5. In Scripture, as far as the east is from the west. Psalm 103. Many shall come from the east and west. Matt. 8.
corruption_summary: The gathering from east and west is read as a promise that all men are saved regardless of repentance and faith, emptying the very sayings in which Christ warns that the children of the kingdom may be cast out.
corruption_paragraphs: The sayings about the gathering from east and west are among the most misused in the Gospels. Because they announce that strangers from every quarter will sit down with Abraham, they are offered as evidence of a final inclusion so wide that repentance and faith become optional and hell empties. The context forbids it flatly. Mat 8:11 is spoken in commendation of a centurion's faith — I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel — and the very next verse continues, but the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness. The saying is not a promise that everyone comes in; it is a warning that descent and religious proximity save nobody while faith brings outsiders to the table. To quote the first half as universalism is to reverse the plain intent of the whole.

The second corruption is subtler and pastoral rather than doctrinal: treating Psa 103:12 as a comforting exaggeration rather than as a measured statement of fact. The psalmist is precise. He does not say our transgressions are removed as far as north is from south, and the omission is deliberate, for north and south meet at the poles and the distance between them can be stated. East and west have no meeting point; travel east forever and you never arrive at west. That is the distance the verse asserts, and it is asserted of a real removal accomplished at real cost. The believer troubled by a sin long ago confessed is not being soothed by a figure of speech; he is being told the location of his guilt, which is nowhere the LORD is willing to look for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew yām means sea, and by orientation west, since the Mediterranean lay westward of Canaan; ma'arāb is the place of the sun's entering, its setting. Greek dusmē is a setting or sinking, used in the plural for the west.
roots_lines: Hebrew yām (H3220) — sea; and by the geography of Canaan, the west or seaward side; the uttermost sea is the western limit of the land (Deu 11:24).
Hebrew ma'arāb (H4628) — the going in of the sun, the west quarter; from 'ārab, to grow dark or become evening.
Greek dusmē (G1424) — a setting, of the sun; used in the plural for the west, as in from the east and west (Mat 8:11).
Hebrew 'acha'rōn — hinder, behind; the western sea is the hinder sea, the observer facing east so that west lies at his back.
The compass pair — east and west form the one axis with no terminus, which is why Psa 103:12 chooses it and not north and south to measure the removal of sin.
usage: Of the measure of pardon: as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us (Psa 103:12).
Of the gathering of the redeemed: I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west (Isa 43:5).
Of outsiders seated and insiders cast out: many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham (Mat 8:11).
scriptures: Psalm 103:12
As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
Isaiah 43:5
Fear not: for I am with thee: I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west;
Genesis 28:14

And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south: and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed.
Matthew 8:11
And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.

etymology: From Old English north, of obscure further origin. The Hebrew tsāphōn is related to a root meaning to hide or lay up in store — the north being the dark quarter, the region the sun never enters, and so the place of what is concealed. Because the great empires that invaded Canaan came down the fertile crescent and entered from the north rather than across the desert, the word acquired a settled prophetic charge: the north is the direction judgment comes from.
biblical_def: North in Scripture is the hidden quarter and the quarter of invasion. Job states the cosmology in a line of striking sobriety: “He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing” (Job 26:7) — the northern heavens spread over emptiness, the earth suspended on no support but the will of God. Because Babylon and Assyria descended on Judah from the north, the prophets use the word as a summons: “Then the LORD said unto me, Out of the north an evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land” (Jer 1:14). Ezekiel's inaugural vision arrives from the same quarter — a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself — so that even the glory of God approaches Judah along the road her enemies use. The north also names a false ambition. In the taunt against the king of Babylon, the sin of the fallen one is put in geographical terms: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north” (Isa 14:13). The mountain of assembly in the far north was, in the mythology of the nations, the seat of deity; the boast is a creature's attempt to occupy God's throne-room, and it is answered by yet thou shalt be brought down to hell. Against that stands Zion, which the psalmist calls beautiful for situation, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King — the true mount of assembly, and God's not by seizure.
webster_summary: One of the cardinal points of the compass, opposite to the south; in Hebrew the hidden or dark quarter; in the prophets the direction from which invading judgment breaks forth; and the region of the boasted throne of Isaiah 14.
webster_full: NORTH, n. 1. One of the cardinal points, being that point of the horizon which is directly opposite to the sun in the meridian.
2. Any region or country situated north of another; as the kings of the north.
3. adj. Being in a point toward the north; as the north side, the north gate, the north wind.
4. In Hebrew, the hidden or dark quarter; from a root signifying to hide or lay up, the sun never entering that region.
5. In Scripture, out of the north an evil shall break forth. Jer. 1. The sides of the north. Isaiah 14; Psalm 48.
corruption_summary: The mount of the congregation in the sides of the north is treated as proof that Scripture simply absorbed Canaanite myth, and the prophetic north as vaticinium after the fact rather than genuine prediction.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure comes from the historical-critical quarter, in two forms. The first argues that because Ugaritic texts locate a divine assembly on a northern mountain, Isa 14:13 shows Israel's Scriptures borrowing pagan cosmology. But the taunt is put in the mouth of the king of Babylon, and the whole force of the passage is that the boast is a lie which God overturns. Isaiah is not endorsing the mythology; he is quoting a pagan aspiration in order to bury it. That surrounding nations had a mountain-of-the-gods tradition is exactly what one expects if the nations retain corrupted memories of the true God, and Psa 48:2 answers them by locating the real city of the great King.

The second form is the dating argument: since Jeremiah's and Ezekiel's northern-invasion oracles match what Babylon actually did, the passages are assumed to have been composed after the event. This assumes precisely what is in question — that predictive prophecy does not occur. The dictionary holds that God declares the end from the beginning, and that the accuracy of a prophecy is evidence of its inspiration rather than of its late composition. The principle to recover is the one Jeremiah himself was given at his call: the LORD watches over His word to perform it, and He announces judgment beforehand so that it may be recognised as His hand and not as accident when it comes.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsāphōn is the north, from a root meaning to hide or store up, the sunless quarter. Greek borras is the north wind and the north. The phrase yark'thē tsāphōn, the sides or uttermost parts of the north, names the mount of assembly.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsāphōn (H6828) — north, the hidden quarter; from tsāphan, to hide, treasure, or lay up in store.
Hebrew yark'thē tsāphōn — the sides, or uttermost parts, of the north; the boasted seat in Isa 14:13 and the true Zion of Psa 48:2.
Hebrew tsāphan (H6845) — to hide or store; thy word have I hid in mine heart (Psa 119:11) uses this root.
Greek borras (G1005) — the north wind, and hence the north quarter; they shall come from the north (Luk 13:29).
Prophetic usage — the invader from the north is Assyria and then Babylon, entering Canaan down the fertile crescent rather than across the eastern desert.
usage: Of the created order: he stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing (Job 26:7).
Of judgment's direction: out of the north an evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land (Jer 1:14).
Of the creature's boast: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north (Isa 14:13).
scriptures: Job 26:7
He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing.
Jeremiah 1:14
Then the LORD said unto me, Out of the north an evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land.
Isaiah 14:13
For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north:
Ezekiel 1:4

And I looked, and, behold, a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire.

pos: n. and adj. (rendering Hebrew negeb, tēmān, and dārōm, Greek notos)
etymology: From Old English sūth, the sun-side, cognate with sun — for an observer in the northern latitudes the sun stands in the southern sky. Hebrew has three words, each with its own flavour: negeb means the parched or dry country, and is the proper name of the arid region south of Judah, which is why the KJV can say a man went up out of Egypt into the south; tēmān means the right hand, the observer facing east; and dārōm is the bright quarter.
biblical_def: South in Scripture is the dry country, the right hand of a man facing the sunrise, and one of the four quarters from which God gathers His people. The patriarchal narratives use it as a place before it is a direction: Abram, driven to Egypt by famine, returns by the same road — “And Abram went up out of Egypt, he, and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the south” (Gen 13:1) — the Negeb being the parched approach to Canaan from Egypt. The word then takes on a theological weight in the psalm that denies every human ladder of advancement: “For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south” (Psa 75:6). The sentence stops short deliberately. Three quarters are named and the fourth is not, because the psalmist will not say that promotion comes from the north either — the next verse supplies the answer that is not a direction at all: but God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another. No point of the compass, no patron, no journey, no alliance lifts a man; God does. And the south stands in the roll of the quarters from which the elect are gathered to the feast: “And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God” (Luk 13:29). It is also the direction of obedience in an unlikely errand, when Philip is sent from a revival to a desert road: “Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert” (Act 8:26).
webster_summary: The point of the compass opposite the north; in Hebrew the dry country, the Negeb south of Judah, and the right hand of one facing east; and in Scripture one of the four quarters from which the redeemed are gathered.
webster_full: SOUTH, n. 1. One of the cardinal points, being the point of the horizon directly opposite to the north.
2. A southern region, country, or place; as, the queen of the south. Matt. 12.
3. adj. Being in a point toward the south; as the south side, the south border, the south wind.
4. In Hebrew, the parched or dry region; the Negeb, lying south of Judah, whence to go into the south is to go into that country.
5. In Scripture, promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. Psalm 75. They shall come from the north, and from the south. Luke 13.
corruption_summary: Advancement is treated as the product of position, patronage, and self-promotion, so that the psalm which denies every earthly source of promotion is quietly reversed into a doctrine of ambition.
corruption_paragraphs: Psa 75:6 is a direct assault on the assumption that governs most of a man's working life: that promotion is a thing to be engineered. The psalmist canvasses the compass and finds it in no quarter, and the answer he gives is not that advancement is unimportant but that its source is a Person. God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another. The corruption is not usually a stated doctrine; it is a practical creed, visible in the energy men spend on visibility and the anxiety they carry about being overlooked. Scripture's counter-command is exact and unfashionable: humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time. The exalting is promised, and it is dated by Someone else.

There is a second and opposite error, which reads such texts as a rebuke to diligence and turns the doctrine of providence into an excuse for passivity — if God alone promotes, effort is presumption. Scripture makes no such inference. Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings. Joseph administered Egypt, Daniel served in a pagan court, and Paul laboured more abundantly than they all. The difference is not between working and not working but between working as a man who must secure his own future and working as a servant whose future is secured, who can therefore take the desert road when he is sent down it (Act 8:26) without calculating what it costs his prospects.
roots_summary: Hebrew negeb is the dry or parched land, and as a proper noun the Negeb south of Judah; tēmān is the right hand, hence the south; dārōm is the bright quarter. Greek notos is the south wind and the south.
roots_lines: Hebrew negeb (H5045) — parched ground, the dry country; the region south of Judah, and by extension the southern quarter.
Hebrew tēmān (H8486) — the right hand, hence the south, the observer being conceived as facing the sunrise.
Hebrew dārōm (H1864) — the south, probably the bright or sunny quarter; used chiefly in Ezekiel and Deuteronomy.
Greek notos (G3558) — the south wind, and the south quarter; the queen of the south (Mat 12:42) and they shall come from the south (Luk 13:29).
Greek mesēmbria (G3314) — midday, and hence the south; the word behind go toward the south in Act 8:26, which may also be read at noon.
usage: Of the dry country of the patriarchs: Abram went up out of Egypt... into the south (Gen 13:1).
Of the source of advancement: promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south (Psa 75:6).
Of the gathering to the feast: they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south (Luk 13:29).
scriptures: Genesis 13:1
And Abram went up out of Egypt, he, and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the south.
Psalm 75:6
For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south.
Luke 13:29
And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God.
Acts 8:26
And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip, saying, Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert.

etymology: From Middle English middest, a superlative of mid — the very middle. Hebrew tāvek is used constantly and idiomatically: to be in the midst of a people is to dwell among them, and the phrase from the midst of is the ordinary way of saying out from among. The word therefore does theological work far beyond its geometry, because the central question of the covenant is whether God is in the midst of His people or has departed from the midst of them.
biblical_def: Midst is the covenant word for the presence of God among His people, and Scripture stations the most decisive things at the centre. The probation of Eden turns on a tree so located: “But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it” (Gen 3:3). The redemption of Israel is described by the same preposition, and it is the boldest sentence in the Exodus: “And the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground: and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left” (Exo 14:22) — the safest place in the world that night was the middle of the sea. The prophets make the presence in the midst the ground of all comfort: “The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing” (Zep 3:17). And the Lord Jesus transfers the promise from a place to Himself and to the gathered church, however small: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20). The last vision keeps the pattern — John turns and sees one like unto the Son of man in the midst of the seven candlesticks, walking among His churches. From tree to sea to tabernacle to congregation to throne, the middle is where God puts what matters, and He is Himself what is put there.
webster_summary: The middle or central part; and in the Scripture idiom, among or in the middle of a company — whence the tree in the midst of the garden, Israel in the midst of the sea, and Christ in the midst of His gathered people.
webster_full: MIDST, n. 1. The middle; used chiefly with a preposition, as in the midst of the day, the midst of the sea.
2. In the Scripture idiom, among; in the middle of a company or multitude. There am I in the midst of them. Matt. 18.
3. The interior or central part of a place; as, in the midst of the garden. Gen. 3.
4. Involved in; surrounded by; as, in the midst of dangers, in the midst of afflictions.
5. In the Hebrew, from the midst of, signifying out from among; as, take the Levites from among the children of Israel. Num. 8.
corruption_summary: Christ's promise to be in the midst of two or three is detached from its context of church discipline and made a sentimental guarantee of atmosphere at any small gathering, while His presence with the great congregation is implicitly denied.
corruption_paragraphs: Mat 18:20 is probably the most frequently misapplied verse in the New Testament. It is regularly quoted to reassure a sparsely attended meeting that Christ is nonetheless present, as though the promise were a consolation for low numbers. Its actual setting is the passage on binding and loosing: a brother has sinned, has refused the private appeal and the appeal before witnesses, and the matter has come before the church. The two or three are the witnesses of verse 16 and the assembly acting in Christ's name, and the promise is that when the church judges according to His word He stands in the midst of the act — His authority behind its verdict. That is a far weightier thing than the sentiment, and considerably more searching, since it means the discipline of a congregation is not a human procedure but one Christ owns.

The misuse also carries an unintended slander. If the promise is read as attaching specially to small gatherings, it quietly implies that Christ is somehow less present where the congregation is large, or that informal fellowship enjoys a nearness that the ordinary assembly under preached word and administered ordinances does not. Scripture gives no such preference. In the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee; He walks in the midst of the seven candlesticks. The principle to recover is that the presence promised is covenantal, not atmospheric — tied to His name, His word, and His appointed means, and therefore neither produced by intimacy nor diminished by numbers.
roots_summary: Hebrew tāvek means the middle, and idiomatically among; the phrase b'thōk is in the midst of and mittōk is out of the midst of. Greek mesos means middle, and en mesō is the corresponding in the midst.
roots_lines: Hebrew tāvek (H8432) — midst, middle, among; one of the commonest nouns in the Old Testament, chiefly in prepositional phrases.
Hebrew b'thōk — in the midst of, among; used of the LORD walking in the midst of the camp (Deu 23:14) and dwelling in the midst of Israel.
Hebrew mittōk — out of the midst of; the voice out of the midst of the fire at Horeb (Deu 4:12), and the call to come out from among them.
Greek mesos (G3319) — middle, midst; en mesō, in the midst, as in Mat 18:20 and Rev 1:13.
Greek mesitos (G3316) — a mediator, literally a middle-man; one that stands in the midst between two parties, of Christ in 1Ti 2:5.
usage: Of the tree of probation: the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden (Gen 3:3).
Of God's saving presence: the LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty (Zep 3:17).
Of Christ among His gathered people: where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them (Mat 18:20).
scriptures: Genesis 3:3
But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die.
Exodus 14:22
And the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground: and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left.
Zephaniah 3:17
The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
Matthew 18:20
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.

etymology: From Old English grund, the bottom or foundation. The Hebrew 'ādāmâh is the tilled, reddish soil, and it stands in a deliberate pun with 'ādām, man: the man is taken from the ground, named for the ground, set to till the ground, cursed in the ground, and returns to the ground. No English rendering can carry the wordplay, but it governs the whole doctrine of man's creaturehood — he is the groundling, and every use of the word in Genesis is pressing that fact upon him.
biblical_def: The ground is where man came from, where his curse fell, where he must stand carefully before God, and where the seed of the gospel is either lost or multiplied. Man is formed of it and bound to it, and when he sinned the sentence did not fall on him alone: “cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life” (Gen 3:17). The thorn and the sweated brow are not incidental to the fall; they are the fall written into the soil, so that a man is reminded of his rebellion every time he works. Ground can also be made holy by the presence of God, and the response required is immediate: “Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” (Exo 3:5). The bush was in an ordinary wilderness; what sanctified the dirt was who stood in it. In the Lord's parables the ground becomes the heart, and the harvest is decided by what kind of ground the word falls into: “But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience” (Luk 8:15). And the ground is finally the place of the death that produces life, which the Lord applied first of all to Himself: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 12:24). Dust, curse, holiness, harvest, and burial — the whole history of man is in this one plain word.
webster_summary: The surface of the earth; soil or mould; the land as tilled; and in Scripture the cursed ground of Adam's labour, the holy ground of God's presence, and the good ground of an honest heart receiving the word.
webster_full: GROUND, n. 1. The surface of the earth or of the terraqueous globe; the earth as we tread upon it.
2. Soil; earth; mould; the substance in which plants take root and grow; as good ground, stony ground.
3. Land; estate; possession; as, he owns a hundred acres of ground.
4. Foundation; that which supports or upholds; hence, the reason or first principle of a thing. The church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. 1 Tim. 3.
5. In Scripture, cursed is the ground for thy sake. Gen. 3. The place whereon thou standest is holy ground. Exod. 3.
corruption_summary: The curse on the ground is dismissed as an aetiological myth explaining why farming is hard, severing the connection between human sin and the disordered creation which Romans 8 makes explicit.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern reading treats Gen 3:17 as an origin-story invented to explain why agriculture is laborious — a pre-scientific people accounting for thorns. On that reading the curse is a description dressed as a sentence, and the moral link between man's rebellion and the world's disorder disappears. Scripture asserts the link as fact and builds doctrine on it: the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope. Paul's whole argument in Rom 8 requires that the groaning of creation be consequent upon Adam's sin and reversible at the revealing of the sons of God. Delete the curse and the promised restoration has nothing to restore, and the resurrection of the body becomes an odd appendix rather than the firstfruits of a renewed earth.

There is a further loss, and it is pastoral. If frustrated labour is simply how the world happens to be, then a man's daily experience of futility — the thorn in every field, the project that will not come right — carries no message. Scripture says it carries a very definite one: it is the ground preaching to the groundling that something is wrong and that he is implicated. That is not a counsel of despair, because the same Scripture sets against Adam's cursed ground the corn of wheat that fell into it willingly and died (Joh 12:24). The ground which swallowed the first man's labour received the last Adam's body, and could not keep it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ādāmâh is tilled soil or ground, punning with 'ādām, man; 'erets is earth or land more broadly. Greek gē is earth, soil, or land, and gives the good ground of the parable of the sower.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ādāmâh (H127) — ground, tilled soil, the reddish earth; man is formed of it (Gen 2:7) and returns to it (Gen 3:19).
Hebrew 'ādām (H120) — man, mankind; the name sounds the ground he was taken from, a pun no translation preserves.
Hebrew 'erets (H776) — earth, land, ground in the wider sense of territory rather than soil.
Greek gē (G1093) — earth, soil, ground, land; the ground of the sower's parable, whether stony, thorny, or good.
Greek hedraiōma (G1477) — a stay or support, rendered ground in the pillar and ground of the truth (1Ti 3:15), a different sense of the English word.
usage: Of the curse on man's labour: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it (Gen 3:17).
Of ground made holy by God's presence: the place whereon thou standest is holy ground (Exo 3:5).
Of the heart receiving the word: that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart... keep it (Luk 8:15).
scriptures: Genesis 3:17

And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;
Exodus 3:5
And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
Luke 8:15
But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience.
John 12:24
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.

etymology: From Old French place, from Latin platea, a broad street or open space, ultimately from Greek plateia, broad. The Hebrew māqōm is built on the verb qūm, to stand or rise up — a place is where a thing stands. That derivation runs quietly under the biblical usage: a man's place is not merely where he happens to be but where he has been set, and the deepest question Scripture asks about place is who assigned it.
biblical_def: Place in Scripture is appointed, not stumbled upon, and the discovery that a place was appointed is one of the recurring surprises of the biblical narratives. Jacob, running for his life with a stone for a pillow, wakes to the recognition: “Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not” (Gen 28:16). He had chosen the spot for no reason but nightfall, and it turned out to be the gate of heaven. Moses is told that the ordinary desert under his feet is not ordinary: “the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” (Exo 3:5). Abraham's obedience is defined by the fact that the place was withheld from him — “when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went” (Heb 11:8) — faith being willingness to be placed by Another. For the wandering people of God the answer to placelessness is not a location but a Person: “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psa 90:1), written by a man who had no fixed address for forty years. And the Lord Jesus makes the preparing of place His own present work: “In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you” (Joh 14:2). Over against every appointed place stands the terrible sentence at the end, where the earth and the heaven flee away and there is found no place for them — the one condition Scripture describes as worse than exile.
webster_summary: A particular portion of space; a locality, spot, or region; a station, rank, or office assigned to a person; and in Scripture the appointed place of God's presence, the place prepared by Christ, and the dwelling place which God Himself is to His people.
webster_full: PLACE, n. 1. A particular portion of space of indefinite extent, occupied or intended to be occupied by any person or thing.
2. Any portion of space, as distinguished from space in general; locality; situation; as the place of a battle.
3. Rank; order of priority or dignity; as, to take the first place in an assembly.
4. Office; employment; official station; as, to hold a place of trust.

5. In Scripture, the appointed spot of God's presence and worship. The place whereon thou standest is holy ground. Exod. 3. I go to prepare a place for you. John 14. Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place. Psalm 90.
corruption_summary: The place Christ went to prepare is dissolved into a state of mind or a symbol of acceptance, so that the plain promise of a prepared dwelling for a resurrected people is treated as too literal to be believed.
corruption_paragraphs: Joh 14:2 is regularly demythologised: the many mansions become a metaphor for spiritual security, and the going to prepare becomes a figure for the psychological comfort the disciples needed. The text resists this at every point. The Lord anticipates the objection Himself — if it were not so, I would have told you — which is a strange thing to say of a metaphor, and He grounds the promise in a bodily journey: I go, and I will come again, and receive you unto myself. The hope of the Christian is not absorption into a state but reception into a house by a Person who left in a body and returns in one. Where the place is spiritualised away, the resurrection of the body loses its point, for a bodiless soul needs no location; and the church loses the concrete future that has sustained its martyrs.

The opposite error is to make place everything — to invest a building, a city, or a plot of ground with the holiness that belongs to God's presence alone, so that pilgrimage to a site becomes a means of grace. The Lord settled this with the woman at the well: neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, shall ye worship the Father. Holy ground was holy because God was standing in it, and Jacob's stone was a gate of heaven because God was there, not because the stone possessed a quality. The principle to recover is that the presence sanctifies the place and never the reverse, which is why a persecuted congregation in a barn is standing on ground as holy as Horeb, and why the God who has been our dwelling place in all generations (Psa 90:1) cannot be left behind when His people are driven out of a country.
roots_summary: Hebrew māqōm is a place or standing-spot, from qūm, to rise or stand; it is the word for the place the LORD chooses to put His name. Greek topos is a place, spot, or opportunity, and gives the room prepared in the Father's house.
roots_lines: Hebrew māqōm (H4725) — place, standing-place, locality; from qūm, to arise or stand, so a place is where a thing stands.
Hebrew hammāqōm 'asher yibchar — the place which the LORD shall choose to put his name there (Deu 12:5); the appointed centre of Israel's worship.
Hebrew mā'ōn (H4583) — a dwelling or habitation; the word behind dwelling place in Psa 90:1.
Greek topos (G5117) — a place, region, or spot; also opportunity or room, as give place unto wrath (Rom 12:19).
Greek monē (G3438) — an abiding place, dwelling, mansion; the many mansions of Joh 14:2, from menō, to abide.
usage: Of a place discovered to be appointed: surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not (Gen 28:16).
Of God Himself as the believer's place: Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations (Psa 90:1).
Of the place Christ prepares: in my Father's house are many mansions... I go to prepare a place for you (Joh 14:2).
scriptures: Genesis 28:16
And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
Exodus 3:5
And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
Psalm 90:1
A Prayer of Moses the man of God. Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.
John 14:2
In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.
